blocks.text: Elsewhere too there is poisonous honey, which drives those who eat it to madness. Such is the honey around Heraclea Pontica, of which Dioscorides ^{e)} and Pliny ^{f)} speak; and that near Trapezus, of which Aristotle ^{g)} and Aelian ^{h)} speak. Many others also mention it, but Xenophon ^{i)} and Diodorus Siculus ^{k)} place it among the Colchians, Strabo ^{l)} among the Heptacometae, and Pliny among the [III, 382] Sanni ^{m)}). From the same author I have learned that poisonous honeycombs are produced also in Persia, and in the Gaetulia of Mauretania Caesariensis bordering on the Massaesylii ^{(7)}. But that bitter honey, or honey in any way defective, is produced in Judaea has never been heard of even in a dream. Indeed in Gen. XLIII, 11. honey is among the מזמרת ארץ, the things praised and celebrated in the land of Canaan ^{(8)}. And the blasphemer Rabshakeh commends Assyria on the ground that, like the land of Canaan, it is fruitful in olives and honey, 2 Reg. XVIII, 32. So in Josephus, book 5 On the War, ch. 4, one of the praises of the territory of Jericho is that it is μελιττοτρόφος ἡ χώρα [melittotrophos hē chōra], a region suited to the rearing of bees. And Alcamus mentions among choice things the Thecoan honey, named after the town of Tekoa, near Jerusalem. His words are: تقوع بالقدس ينسب اليه العسل [Taqūʿ bi-l-Quds yunsabu ilayhi al-ʿasal] Tekoa, a town near Kuds (that is, Jerusalem), after which honey is named, or else whose honey is renowned. Accordingly honey was exported from Judaea to other lands: to the markets of the Tyrians, Ezech. XXVII, 17. and to Egypt, Gen. XLIII, 11. Although we also read that Egypt itself abounded in honey, Num. XVI, 13. Nor should anyone imagine that these things are said only of domestic honey. [col. 522] For wild was the honey whose sweetness Samson extolled in such splendid words, Iud. XIV, 14. And so was that other honey, on tasting which Jonathan's eyes were opened, 1 Sam. 14. 29. Wild also was the honey of the rock, that is, honey flowing from the clefts of rocks in which wild bees made their honey. Yet it is counted among the delights that God offered to his people, Deut. XXXII, 13. He made him ride on the high places of the earth, that he might eat the produce of the fields, and he gave him honey to suck from the rock. Psalm. LXXXI, 17. He will feed him with the fat of wheat, and with honey from the rock he will satisfy him. Thus both in wild [III, 383] and in domestic honey there was what pleased the palate. Yet in John the Baptist it was a mark of great abstinence that he lived on locusts and wild honey alone: because, as in locusts (as was proved in its place), so also in honey there is little nourishment when it is taken alone and by itself. Hippocrates, ch. 50 On Affections: Τὸ μέλι, ξὺν ἑτέροις ἐσθιόμενον, καὶ τρέφει· καὶ εὔχροιαν παρέχει. Αὐτὸ δὲ ἐφ᾽ ἑαυτῷ λεπτύνει μᾶλλον, ἢ κομίζει [To meli, xyn heterois esthiomenon, kai trephei; kai euchroian parechei. Auto de eph᾽ heautō leptynei mallon, ē komizei], Honey, eaten with other things, both nourishes and gives a good colour. But by itself it rather thins than restores. The ancients celebrate the abstinence of Aristoxenus, the Cyrenaic philosopher, on the ground that θρίδακα ἐν κήπῳ οἰνομέλιτι ποτίζων ἑσπέρας, καὶ ὑπὸ τὴν ἕω λαμβάνων, χλωροὺς ἔχειν ἔλεγε πλακοῦντας [thridaka en kēpō oinomeliti potizōn hesperas, kai hypo tēn heō lambanōn, chlōrous echein elege plakountas], watering lettuce in his garden with honeyed wine towards evening and taking it in the morning, he said he had yellow cakes. And that of Pythagoras, because εὐτελέστατα διαβιοὺς, πολλάκις μέλιτι μόνῳ ἠρκεῖτο [eutelestata diabious, pollakis meliti monō ērkeito], he lived so frugally that he was often content with honey alone. So Eustathius reports on Iliad λ΄ [11]. But our John far surpasses both. For Aristoxenus added wine and lettuce to the honey, from which John abstained. And Pythagoras was content with honey alone often, yet not always. For Laertius says of him: Ἐνίοτε δὲ αὐτὸν ἀρκεῖσθαι μέλιτι μόνῳ φασί τινες, ἢ κηρίῳ, ἢ ἄρτῳ· οἴνου δὲ μεθ᾽ ἡμέραν μὴ γεύσασθαι· ὄψον τε τὰ πολλὰ λαχάνοις ἑφθοῖς, καὶ ὠμοῖς, τοῖς δὲ θαλαττίοις σπανίως [Eniote de auton arkeisthai meliti monō phasi tines, ē kēriō, ē artō; oinou de meth᾽ hēmeran mē geusasthai; opson te ta polla lachanois hephthois, kai ōmois, tois de thalattiois spaniōs]. Some say that he sometimes lived content with honey alone, or a honeycomb, or bread; but that during the day (that is, until evening) he did not taste wine; and that for relish he mostly had boiled or raw vegetables, and seldom used seafood. Moreover, these men ate purchased food, whereas John fed on whatever chance offered, relying so firmly on God's providence that in the desert he depended on it alone, certain that the things necessary to sustain life would not fail him.
